strengths: Compelling and coherent formulation for 4D human-scene reconstruction from monocular in-the-wild videos, addressing the mutual dependencies between camera pose, dense scene geometry, and global human motion.
Principled integration of physical human-scene contact constraints (contact scale loss and contact static loss) to ground human motion and resolve metric scale ambiguities in scene reconstruction.

Significant empirical performance gains over state-of-the-art baselines across multiple challenging datasets (EMDB, SLOPER4D, RICH) in both global human motion estimation (e.g., reducing W-MPJPE on EMDB from 222.4 mm to 174.7 mm and on SLOPER4D from 1005.3 mm to 438.3 mm) and metric dense reconstruction.

Practical distillation of the optimization framework into an end-to-end feed-forward model (JOSH3R) trained on pseudo-labels generated by JOSH, demonstrating real-time inference (15.4 FPS) with competitive accuracy.
Clear writing, well-structured ablation studies validating each loss component and architectural choice, and informative qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: High reliance on a complex cascade of off-the-shelf pre-trained components (MASt3R, DEVA/segmentation, SMPL recovery models, and BSTRO contact detector), where cascading errors or inaccurate initial contact predictions could negatively impact optimization convergence.

The 2D nearest neighbor heuristic used to find contact correspondences in the background point cloud ($x_s^t = \arg\min_{x^t \in \tilde{X}^t} |\pi_t(x^t) - \pi_t(x_h^t)|_2$) may be prone to mismatches in cluttered scenes, severe occlusion, or non-planar contact geometries.

Performance of the real-time model JOSH3R drops considerably compared to the optimization-based JOSH (e.g., WA-MPJPE increases from 120.0 to 271.1 mm on SLOPER4D), indicating that full feed-forward modeling remains a significant challenge.
JOSH optimization remains computationally demanding (0.8 FPS), limiting its immediate applicability to very long video sequences without segmenting into short chunks.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated framework tackling the challenging task of unified 4D human-scene reconstruction from monocular in-the-wild videos, explicitly exploiting the mutual physical constraints between humans and environments.

Formulation of human-scene contact losses (contact scale and contact static losses) effectively bridges MASt3R-based dense scene reconstruction and global SMPL motion optimization, resolving metric scale ambiguity and foot sliding.

Outstanding empirical results across three standard benchmarks (EMDB, SLOPER4D, RICH), significantly outperforming previous state-of-the-art methods in global human motion estimation (e.g., cutting W-MPJPE on SLOPER4D from 1272.3 mm to 438.3 mm) and camera pose/scene reconstruction.

The introduction of JOSH3R demonstrates a practical trade-off, showing that pseudo-labels generated by the optimization pipeline can train an end-to-end model capable of running at interactive frame rates (15.4 FPS) while remaining competitive with other optimization-free baselines.
The paper is clearly written, logically structured, and supported by thorough ablation studies and qualitative visualizations.
weaknesses: High pipeline complexity: JOSH relies on an extensive stack of pre-trained off-the-shelf models for initialization (MASt3R for scene/camera, DEVA/VitDet for segmentation/tracking, VIMO/SMPLer-X for camera-frame HMR, and BSTRO for contact prediction), which introduces many potential points of failure if initial predictions are noisy.

Heuristic contact matching: The contact association relies on searching for the nearest static scene pixel in 2D projection space. In scenarios with complex geometry, occlusions, or steep perspective angles, 2D proximity does not necessarily imply true 3D spatial contact.

Significant performance drop from JOSH to JOSH3R: While JOSH3R achieves real-time inference, its quantitative accuracy lags far behind full JOSH optimization (e.g., W-MPJPE of 1217.1 mm vs. 438.3 mm on SLOPER4D, and 661.7 mm vs. 174.7 mm on EMDB), highlighting generalization challenges across different domain distributions.
Computational overhead of JOSH: Optimization takes approximately 0.8 FPS and requires processing in 100-frame windows, limiting its applicability for immediate or interactive use cases.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely task: 4D human-scene reconstruction in the wild from monocular video by tightly coupling global human motion estimation with dense metric scene reconstruction.

The formulation of human-scene contact losses (contact scale loss and contact static loss) provides an effective physical inductive bias that successfully anchors metric scale and mitigates sliding artifacts.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmark datasets (EMDB, SLOPER4D, RICH) demonstrating clear state-of-the-art performance against both dedicated global HMR methods (WHAM, TRAM) and dense scene reconstruction baselines (MASt3R, MonST3R).

The exploration of JOSH3R—distilling the iterative optimization pipeline into a real-time (15.4 FPS) feed-forward model trained solely on pseudo-labels from web videos—is a practical and promising direction for scaling 4D reconstruction.
weaknesses: High dependence on multiple off-the-shelf pre-trained models: the pipeline requires external models for video segmentation (DEVA), camera-frame human mesh recovery (VIMO/SMPLer-X), dense geometry initialization (MASt3R), and per-vertex contact prediction (BSTRO). Optimization quality is inherently vulnerable to cascading failures in any of these upfront estimators.

The heuristic for establishing contact correspondences—matching predicted contact vertices to scene points by nearest 2D projected pixel distance—is prone to mismatches in cluttered scenes, complex occlusions, or extreme perspective foreshortening where points are visually close in 2D but separated in depth.

Limited generalization and domain gap in JOSH3R: because JOSH3R is trained on a relatively homogeneous set of 13 urban walking videos, its performance on datasets with varied viewpoints and dynamics (such as EMDB in Table 5) degrades noticeably (e.g., WA-MPJPE of 220.0 compared to WHAM's 131.1 and TRAM's 76.4).

Minor clarity and presentation issues: in Section A of the Supplementary Material, it states for the second optimization stage: 'further refines the results with the 2D projection loss by setting w2D = 0', which appears to be a typo for a positive weight value.

strengths: Holistic formulation: Tackles monocular 4D human-scene reconstruction by jointly optimizing dense scene geometry, camera poses, camera intrinsics (focal length), and multi-human motion in a single stage, moving beyond traditional disjoint pipelines.

Effective contact constraints: The proposed contact scene loss and contact static loss effectively exploit estimated contact regions to ground human motion, which notably improves physical plausibility (drastically reducing foot sliding, jitter, and foot floating rate).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is validated across multiple benchmarks (SLOPER4D, EMDB, RICH) and across various initialization pairings (HMR2.0/DROID-SLAM, WHAM/MonST3R, VIMO/MASt3R), consistently outperforming prior baselines such as SynCHMR, SLAHMR, and TRAM in both motion accuracy and scene reconstruction quality.

Downstream utility via pseudo-labeling: Demonstrates that JOSH can be utilized as a pseudo-label generator on unlabeled web video to train an end-to-end model (JOSH3R), showing promise for scaling 4D human-scene modeling.
weaknesses: Heavy dependency on multi-stage pre-trained models: The initialization pipeline relies on a large stack of external off-the-shelf tools (DEVA for segmentation, BSTRO for contact prediction, ZoeDepth for depth, ViTPose for 2D keypoints, plus HMR and SfM backbones). A failure or severe bias in one of these upstream components can negatively propagate into the joint optimization.

Heuristic contact correspondence matching: The contact point association between the SMPL mesh and dense point cloud relies on 2D reprojection proximity and monocular depth filtering (|Z(x_s) - Z(x_h)| < ϵ). This heuristic may become fragile under depth ambiguities, non-planar/complex geometries, or hand/object interactions.

Computational overhead and scalability: The iterative joint optimization runs at only ~0.8 FPS (as reported in Table 3) and requires breaking videos into short 100-frame chunks with keyframe downsampling, making it computationally expensive for processing long video collections.

Performance gap with the feed-forward model: While JOSH3R demonstrates real-time inference (15.4 FPS), its estimation accuracy lags noticeably behind the optimization-based JOSH (e.g., Table 3 shows JOSH3R achieves 661.7 mm W-MPJPE on EMDB compared to 174.7 mm for JOSH3), indicating that directly regressing relative human transformation without bundle adjustment remains challenging.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated framework: Jointly optimizing camera poses, dense scene geometry, and 4D global human motion in a single stage effectively resolves the metric scale ambiguity and physically implausible artifacts (such as foot sliding and ground penetration) common to decoupled pipelines.

Effective contact-grounded loss formulations: The proposed contact scene loss ($L_{c1}$) and contact static loss ($L_{c2}$) provide physically intuitive geometric anchors between the foreground human body vertices and dense background scene points, substantially improving both human motion and scene reconstruction accuracy.

Comprehensive and multi-faceted empirical evaluation: The approach is evaluated across three diverse benchmarks (SLOPER4D, EMDB, and RICH) across multiple facets—human pose/trajectory metrics, scene reconstruction metrics (ATE, Chamfer Distance), and physical plausibility metrics (jitter, foot sliding, foot floating rate).

Generality across frontends: The authors validate the framework across different initialization backbones (HMR2.0, WHAM, VIMO for human pose; DROID-SLAM, MonST3R, MASt3R for scene reconstruction), demonstrating consistent and significant gains regardless of the initialization source.

Scalable end-to-end proof of concept (JOSH3R): Demonstrating that JOSH can be used to generate reliable pseudo-labels on 20 hours of in-the-wild web videos to train a feed-forward model (JOSH3R) operating at 15.4 FPS offers a viable and scalable path forward for the field.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on a complex cascade of pre-trained tools: JOSH relies on off-the-shelf models for human mesh recovery, dense scene reconstruction/matching, video segmentation (DEVA), 2D keypoints (ViTPose), depth priors (ZoeDepth), and contact estimation (BSTRO). While Appendix F evaluates robustness under synthetic noise, failures in upstream modules (such as missed contacts or segmentation errors under heavy occlusion) could cause compounding failures.

Contact correspondence heuristic: The correspondence between predicted human contact vertices and scene contact points relies on nearest-neighbor search in 2D projection gated by a monocular depth tolerance ($|\hat{Z}^t(x_s) - \hat{Z}^t(x_h)| < \epsilon$). In scenes with high depth discontinuities, fine foliage, or cluttered objects near contact surfaces, this heuristic may produce false associations.
Optimization throughput: Optimizing a 100-frame chunk with 1000 iterations runs at approximately 0.8 FPS, limiting JOSH's utility to offline batch processing.

Limited quantitative multi-person benchmark evaluation: Although the methodology supports multi-person optimization, the core quantitative benchmarks (SLOPER4D, EMDB, RICH) predominantly focus on single moving subjects. Additional quantitative evaluation on crowded in-the-wild video benchmarks with mutual human occlusions would strengthen the multi-human claims.
Minor presentation flaws: Figure 1 has minor typesetting artifacts (truncated/overlapping text fragments like 'n Estimation Dense Scene Reconstruction' at the top).

strengths: Holistic joint optimization formulation: Unlike existing methods that perform disjoint or sequential estimation of camera poses, scene geometry, and human trajectory, JOSH integrates human-scene contact constraints (contact scene loss and contact static loss) to jointly refine camera, dense scene points, and SMPL body parameters in a single unified stage.

Comprehensive empirical validation: The method is benchmarked across three standard datasets (SLOPER4D, EMDB, RICH) across diverse evaluation axes, including global motion metrics (WA-MPJPE, W-MPJPE, RTE), dense 3D scene reconstruction metrics (Chamfer Distance, depth AbsRel, ATE), and physical plausibility metrics (foot sliding, jitter, foot floating rate).

Modularity across backbones: The paper evaluates JOSH across multiple initialization baselines (HMR2.0, WHAM, VIMO for human motion; DROID-SLAM, MonST3R, MASt3R for scene reconstruction), consistently demonstrating performance gains regardless of the underlying initialization network.

Web-scale pseudo-labeling demonstration: The authors show that JOSH can generate pseudo-labels on ~20 hours of in-the-wild web video to train a feed-forward model (JOSH3R), establishing the practical utility of the optimization pipeline for scalable data generation.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on a multi-stage pipeline of off-the-shelf models: The initialization depends on multiple separate external models (DEVA for segmentation, BSTRO for contact prediction, ViTPose for 2D keypoints, ZoeDepth/monocular depth priors, plus local HMR and scene reconstruction backbones). Failures in upstream contact estimation or dynamic masking can degrade downstream optimization.

Contact-dependent formulation: The core synergy bridging scene geometry and human trajectories relies on visible, static human-scene contact points (primarily feet/hands). In sequences where subjects are moving without firm static ground contact (e.g., jumping, swimming, riding vehicles) or when contact points are occluded, the key regularizing constraints become significantly less effective.

Computational overhead of test-time optimization: Running 1,000 optimization iterations per 100-frame window yields an amortized speed of approximately 0.8 FPS, which restricts real-time application and makes processing large-scale video corpora computationally demanding.

Limited quantitative evaluation on multi-human scenarios: Although the paper highlights multi-human reconstruction as a capability, the quantitative evaluations on SLOPER4D, EMDB, and RICH are predominantly evaluated on single-subject sequences. A formal quantitative evaluation specifically measuring multi-person relative spatial consistency is lacking.
